title: Visualization of naive and learned odor representations using in vivo calcium imaging and immunohistochemical bouton mapping of single Drosophila mushroom body neurons
protocol: Select a single transgenic female fly from the previous steps.
Place the selected fly in an empty plastic vial on ice.
Keep the fly on ice for 5 minutes to anaesthetize it.
Fix the fly in a custom-built imaging chamber using clear adhesive tape.
Cut a hole in the adhesive tape to expose only the head of the fly.
Use blue light-curing glue to fix the head on the back and sides.
Apply a drop of room temperature Ringer’s solution on the exposed head cuticle.
Open the head capsule using a fine bladed knife.
Remove the cuticle and any excess tissue that lies on top of the brain.
Prepare the odor mixtures using MCH, 3-octanol, and 1-octanol in mineral oil at concentrations of 1:750, 1:500, and 1:400 respectively.
Install odors in the odor delivery system.
Place the prepared fly under a microscope equipped for two-photon imaging.
Illuminate the preparation using a red filter set.
Observe the fly brain through the eyepieces for expression of mCherry in Kenyon cells.
Ensure that only flies with a maximum of 3 Kenyon cells per hemisphere are labelled can be utilized.
Position the fly head in the center of the field of view for imaging.
Place the odor delivery system in position.
Connect electrical wires to a power source.
Limit external light sources as much as possible.
Start the microscope control software.
Initialize image acquisition settings.
Set an excitation wavelength of 940 nm.
Use a customized filter set with a 605 nm beamsplitter and two bandpass filters: one for mCherry detection (620–680 nm) and another for GFP detection (500–550 nm).
Locate the labelled Kenyon cells.
Crop and rotate the acquisition region to center the Kenyon cells.
Run a synchronized image acquisition sequence with odor presentation through multiple z-planes.
Present all odors and mineral oil via air stream in each imaging plane at a flow rate of 1 mL/s.
Capture between 4 and 7 imaging planes per brain, depending on cell number and anatomical complexity.
Use a framerate of 4 Hz for image acquisition.
Save the image sequences for later analysis.
Run the associative conditioning protocol.
Present one odor continuously for 60 seconds with overlapping pulsing electric shocks.
Pause for 60 seconds, then present a second odor for 60 seconds without electric shocks.
For CS-only control groups, omit the electric shock during odor presentation.
For unpaired control groups, deliver the electric shock 2 minutes before the onset of the first odor.
Repeat the odor presentation protocol to collect post-training data.
Ensure measurements are conducted in the same imaging planes as before conditioning.
Capture a z-stack covering the entire depth of the brain after all planes have been measured.
Remove the imaging chamber from the microscope with the fly intact.
Proceed to remove the brain for immunohistochemical staining.
Carefully remove the fly from the imaging chamber.
Transfer the fly to a dissection dish containing a black-dyed silicon mixture.
Fix the fly in place, ventral side up, using insect pins through the thorax and abdomen.
Cover the fly with 2–3 drops of ice-cold Ringer’s solution.
Remove the proboscis carefully using fine forceps.
Pull apart the two sides of the head capsule until completely removed from the brain.
Clear away residual tissues from the brain.
Detach the brain from the thorax, leaving behind the ventral nerve cord.
Place the brain in fixative solution (4% paraformaldehyde in PBS) for 2 hours on a shaker at 4°C.
Wash the brain three times for 20 minutes each in PBS-T washing solution at room temperature on a shaker.
Place the brain in blocking solution (2% bovine serum albumin in PBS-T) for 2 hours on a shaker at room temperature.
Transfer the brain to a dish containing a primary antibody mix with rabbit anti-GFP and mouse anti-DLG antibodies.
Incubate the brain on a shaker at 4°C for 12–16 hours.
Wash the brain as in step 24.
Transfer the brains to a dish containing a secondary antibody mix.
Incubate on a shaker at 4°C for 12–16 h.
Wash the brain as in step 24.
Pipette approximately 5 μL of VectaShield into a 13 mm tape ring.
Carefully place the brain in the liquid, orienting it so that it lays flat with the anterior facing upwards.
Scan the brain using a confocal laser scanning microscope.
Choose laser and detector settings according to the secondary antibodies used.
Install an image processing program such as ImageJ.
Open the installed image processing program.
Correct each image series for movement in X and Y dimensions using TurboReg or a similar plug-in.
Mark regions of interest (ROIs) encompassing individual synaptic boutons along Kenyon cell axons pre- and post-training.
Ensure that only boutons identifiable in both recordings are used for analysis.
Extract fluorescence intensity values over time for the green (GCaMP) and red (mCherry) channels using the “Multi Measure” function.
Calculate ΔF/F0 values from raw fluorescence data.
Generate F0 value by calculating the average fluorescence from 5 seconds preceding odor onset.
Generate ΔF values by subtracting F0 value from raw fluorescence.
Divide ΔF value at each frame by F0 to generate a ΔF/F0 trace over time.
Apply a 3-frame moving average through the time series to filter the ΔF/F0 trace temporally.
Subtract the mCherry ΔF/F0 from the GCaMP ΔF/F0 to reduce fluctuations due to preparation movement.
Open confocal image stacks of immunostained brain in ImageJ.
Use mCherry and GFP image stacks to track Kenyon cell(s) through the image stacks.
Generate a 3-dimensional projection view of the Kenyon cell(s).
Translate bouton positions from functional imaging view (dorsal) to anatomical imaging view (anterior).
Separate distinct Kenyon cells if necessary, forming separate projections for each cell.
Map the identified boutons onto anatomical images using the z-stack generated during functional imaging.
Exclude boutons for which positions cannot be translated to anatomical images from analysis.
Using anti-DLG neuropil staining, identify the 5 compartments of the mushroom body γ-lobe.
Note the compartment location of each measured bouton within the identified compartments.
Calculate the Michelson contrast of the two amplitudes using the formula provided.
Set the contrast value to 1 if there is no difference between both responses.
Adjust the contrast value towards 0 as the responses become more dissimilar.
Introduce a third term that calculates the mean response of two boutons, normalized by the maximum response of the neuron.
Set flat responses to 0 in the calculation.
Assign robust responses values close to 1 based on their amplitude.
Multiply each of the three measures (cross correlation, amplitude contrast, and normalized mean amplitude) to derive a sensitive measure for quantifying congruence.

Feature selection involves identifying characteristic quantifiable parameters of the data set.
In this study, peak amplitude (ΔF/F0) and latency to the peak are used as features.
Agglomerative hierarchical clustering treats each bouton response as an individual cluster initially.
The algorithm calculates Euclidean distances between data samples.
Clusters are merged using Ward’s criterion to prioritize minimal within-cluster variance.
Each sample is assigned to a specific cluster, resulting in the assignment of each observed bouton response to a BRC.
